answer: I would like to talk about a teacher who, in a way, is part of the reason I can speak English today. The teacher who influenced me most was my secondary school English teacher, who genuinely changed how I saw the subject. Before her class, I found English dull and mechanical, just grammar rules to memorise for exams. She taught us English language and literature for two years, and she had this gift for making lessons feel [[engaging]], often using stories, songs and debates instead of dry exercises. Sometimes she would ask us to act out scenes from short stories, which felt terrifying at first but was great fun, and it made the language feel alive for the first time. What set her apart was her genuine belief in her students; she could spot potential we could not see in ourselves. She was also endlessly [[encouraging]], praising effort rather than just results, which built my confidence enormously. As for how she influenced me, I still remember how she pushed me to enter a writing competition I would never have attempted alone. I did not win, but I was shortlisted, and that small success meant the world to me. That single act of [[faith]] in me changed my relationship with the language completely. Honestly, a large part of why I am comfortable using English today is [[attributable]] to her, including in my job, where I use it every single day. I think great teachers do exactly this: they light a spark that keeps burning long after the classroom.

followUps.q: Are you still in touch with her?
followUps.answer: Sadly not directly, as she moved to another district some years ago. But I heard through a friend that she is still teaching, and I like to think she is still [[igniting]] that same spark in her students.

followUps.q: Do you think teachers are more important than textbooks?
followUps.answer: Definitely. A textbook gives you information, but a good teacher gives you the motivation to use it. I think most people remember a great teacher far longer than any book they studied.
